title: IS GOD REALLY COMMANDING YOU TO KEEP THE SABBATH—OR ARE YOU CARRYING A BURDEN JESUS NEVER PLACED ON YOU?
paragraphs: IS GOD REALLY COMMANDING YOU TO KEEP THE SABBATH—OR ARE YOU CARRYING A BURDEN JESUS NEVER PLACED ON YOU?

The Fourth Commandment. The Forgotten Seventh Day. The Resurrection of Jesus. And the Uncomfortable Question Every Christian Must Face: Is Sabbath-Keeping Still Binding, or Has Christ Fulfilled Something Far Greater?
There is a Christian somewhere reading this with a troubled conscience.
They love Jesus. They read their Bible. They pray. They want to obey God.
But every time Saturday comes, something happens inside them.
A question.
A fear.
A quiet accusation.
What if I've been disobeying God all these years?

Perhaps someone told them that Sunday worship is a human invention. That the Sabbath was never abolished. That the fourth commandment is still written in stone, and that anyone who truly loves God must worship on the seventh day.
Then another Christian tells them the opposite.
We're under grace, not the law. Jesus fulfilled the Sabbath. You don't have to keep Saturday.
Both open their Bibles.
Both quote Scripture.
Both claim to honor Jesus.
And somewhere between their arguments stands an ordinary believer who simply wants to know the truth.
Maybe that believer is you.
But before you decide which side is right, consider something that might change the entire conversation.
What if the greatest danger is not choosing the wrong day, but misunderstanding the Savior to whom the Sabbath was always pointing?
Don't rush past that question.

Because the answer will take us from the opening chapters of Genesis to Mount Sinai, from the wilderness of Israel to the accusations of the Pharisees, from an empty tomb in Jerusalem to a promise of rest that reaches beyond any twenty-four-hour period.
And somewhere along the way, we must confront a truth that neither careless lawlessness nor religious legalism can afford to ignore.
God's commandments matter.
Grace matters.
And Jesus Christ must remain at the center of both.
The story begins before there was a nation called Israel.
Before Moses climbed Sinai.
Before the Ten Commandments were written.
Before the first synagogue ever existed.
Genesis 2:2–3 tells us that God finished His work of creation, rested on the seventh day, and blessed and sanctified that day.
The Hebrew word translated rested comes from שָׁבַת (shavat), meaning to cease or desist.
God did not rest because He was exhausted.
The Almighty does not become weary.
Isaiah 40:28 makes that clear.
God ceased from His creative work because it was complete.
The seventh day was blessed and set apart.
That matters enormously.
The Sabbath did not originate as an arbitrary religious invention. Its foundation lies in God's own creation pattern.
But we must also notice what Genesis does not explicitly say.
Genesis 2 does not record a direct command requiring Adam and Eve, or every subsequent human being, to observe a weekly Sabbath with the regulations later given to Israel.

Some Christians understand the sanctification of the seventh day as establishing a creation ordinance binding on all humanity. Others understand it as the theological foundation for the Sabbath command that would later be given to Israel.
Both perspectives take the passage seriously.
The disagreement is not whether God blessed the seventh day.
He did.
The question is whether that blessing, by itself, establishes an unchanged weekly legal obligation for every Christian under the new covenant.
That question cannot be settled by ignoring the rest of Scripture.
Now imagine the people of Israel.
Generations of slavery.
Bricks.
Whips.
Forced labor.
Days measured by production.
Human worth reduced to usefulness.
Then God delivers them.
The God who heard their cries leads them out of Egypt.
And to these former slaves, He gives something astonishing.
Rest.
Exodus 20:8 declares:
"Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy."
The Hebrew reads:
זָכוֹר אֶת־יוֹם הַשַּׁבָּת לְקַדְּשׁוֹ
Zakhor et-yom haShabbat leqaddesho.
Remember the Sabbath day, to sanctify it.
This is not a suggestion.
It is a command.
And Exodus 20:10 identifies the seventh day as the Sabbath of the LORD.
We should never minimize that.
God commanded Israel to stop working, and the command extended beyond the individual Israelite to children, servants, livestock, and foreigners residing within their gates.
Think about the compassion embedded in that command.
In Egypt, the powerful determined when the weak could rest.
Under God's covenant, even servants were given protection from endless labor.
The Sabbath proclaimed that human beings were not created merely to produce.
Their lives belonged to God.
And in Deuteronomy 5:12–15, Moses connects Sabbath observance not only with creation but also with Israel's deliverance from slavery.
The Sabbath remembered both the Creator and the Redeemer.
But here is where we must be careful.

A command can be genuinely holy, divinely inspired, and binding upon the people to whom God gave it without necessarily retaining the identical covenantal function after Christ establishes the new covenant.
Consider circumcision.
God commanded it as the covenant sign given to Abraham and his descendants in Genesis 17.
It was not an evil practice.
It was commanded by God.
Yet Acts 15 and Galatians 5 make clear that Gentile believers are not required to receive circumcision as a condition of belonging to God's covenant people.
The question was never whether God had commanded circumcision.
He had.
The question was how that command related to the saving work of Jesus Christ and the inclusion of Gentiles under the new covenant.
The Sabbath question demands similar care.
Exodus 31:13 describes Israel's Sabbaths as a sign between God and the people of Israel.
Exodus 31:16–17 explicitly identifies the Sabbath as a sign of the covenant between the LORD and Israel.
That covenantal setting cannot simply be erased.
Yet neither should the creation foundation of the Sabbath be dismissed.
This is why faithful Christians have reached different conclusions.
Some believe the weekly Sabbath remains a moral obligation rooted in creation and reaffirmed in the Ten Commandments.
Some believe the weekly day of rest continues as a moral principle but is observed on the Lord's Day, Sunday, in celebration of Christ's resurrection.
Others believe the Sabbath's binding covenantal requirement has been fulfilled in Christ, leaving believers free to observe a day voluntarily without making it a universal requirement.
We must examine these views by Scripture rather than assuming that the loudest voice must be the most biblical.
And then Jesus enters the story.
Not as a detached commentator.
Not as another rabbi offering one more opinion.
But as the Son of God.
The One through whom all things were made.
The One who would fulfill the Law and the Prophets.
One Sabbath, Jesus' disciples plucked grain as they walked through the fields.
The Pharisees objected.
They accused the disciples of doing what was unlawful on the Sabbath.
Jesus answered by referring to David and the consecrated bread, and then He spoke words that should make every religious heart pay attention.
Mark 2:27–28 records:
"The sabbath was made for man, and not man for the sabbath: Therefore the Son of man is Lord also of the sabbath."
The Greek expression is:
τὸ σάββατον διὰ τὸν ἄνθρωπον ἐγένετο
To sabbaton dia ton anthrōpon egeneto.
The Sabbath came into being for the sake of humanity.
The word ἄνθρωπον (anthrōpon) refers to a human being or humanity in this context.
Jesus was exposing a terrible reversal.
A gift intended for human good had become, in the hands of some religious authorities, an instrument of accusation.
The Sabbath was meant to serve God's gracious purposes.
It was not meant to crush the people it was designed to bless.
But notice something important.
Jesus did not say that the Sabbath was meaningless.
Nor did He explicitly announce in Mark 2 that the fourth commandment had been abolished.
Instead, He asserted His authority over it.
The Son of Man is Lord even of the Sabbath.
That declaration changes everything.
Because the ultimate authority for understanding the Sabbath is not a religious institution, a denomination, a church tradition, or a popular online preacher.
It is Jesus Christ.
And what did Jesus do on the Sabbath?
He healed.
He restored.
He liberated.
In Luke 13, Jesus encountered a woman who had been bent over for eighteen years.
Eighteen years.
Imagine her waking every morning unable to stand upright.
Imagine the pain.
The embarrassment.
The exhaustion of living inside a body that would not cooperate.
Jesus saw her.
And on the Sabbath, He called her forward and healed her.
The synagogue ruler objected because the healing had taken place on the Sabbath.
But Jesus confronted the hypocrisy.
If people could untie an animal to give it water on the Sabbath, should not this daughter of Abraham be released from her bondage?
Luke 13:16 describes her as someone Satan had bound for eighteen years.
And Jesus set her free.
Do you see the beauty?
The Lord of the Sabbath was standing before a woman whose life had become a prison.
And He did not tell her to return tomorrow.
He restored her that day.
The Sabbath, in the hands of Jesus, became a setting for mercy, liberation, and the revelation of God's kingdom.
But the story does not end there.
Because a greater liberation was approaching.
And it would require a cross.
Jesus declared in Matthew 5:17:
"Think not that I am come to destroy the law, or the prophets: I am not come to destroy, but to fulfil."
The Greek verb translated fulfil is πληρῶσαι (plērōsai).
It carries the sense of bringing something to fullness or completion.
But fulfillment must not be confused with simply declaring every command irrelevant.
Jesus' fulfillment of the Law and the Prophets includes bringing their purposes and promises to their intended goal.
He does not authorize sin.
He does not dismiss holiness.
He does not make obedience meaningless.
In the Sermon on the Mount, He actually deepens the moral demands of God's will, confronting anger, lust, dishonesty, retaliation, and hatred.
Yet the New Testament also teaches that the coming of Christ transforms the covenantal relationship of God's people to the Mosaic law.
Hebrews 8:13 speaks of the old covenant becoming obsolete in light of the new.
Romans 7:6 describes believers as released from the law in the sense explained by Paul's argument, so that they serve in the new way of the Spirit.
Galatians warns against making observance of Mosaic covenant requirements the basis of justification.
Therefore, saying that Christ fulfilled the law is not the same as saying Christians may live however they please.
And saying Christians must pursue holiness is not the same as saying every Mosaic covenant regulation remains binding in precisely the same form.
We need to make these distinctions because Scripture makes them.
Now we arrive at one of the most decisive passages in the discussion.
Colossians 2:16–17.
Paul writes:
The Greek includes:
ἑορτῆς ἢ νεομηνίας ἢ σαββάτων
Heortēs ē neomēnias ē sabbatōn.
Festival, new moon, or Sabbaths.
The sequence resembles Old Testament descriptions of annual, monthly, and weekly sacred observances, as found in passages such as 1 Chronicles 23:31 and Ezekiel 45:17.
For this reason, many interpreters understand Paul's reference to include the weekly Sabbath.
Others argue that Paul is addressing particular ceremonial observances or the misuse of Sabbath regulations within the Colossian controversy, not overturning the weekly Sabbath command itself.
The disagreement deserves acknowledgment.
But Paul's central instruction is unmistakable.
Do not allow someone to judge your standing before God on the basis of the observances he is discussing.
Why?
Because those things were a shadow.
The Greek word is σκιὰ (skia).
A shadow.
And the reality to which the shadow points belongs to Christ.
Imagine waiting years for someone you love to come home.
You have their photograph.
You hold it when you miss them.
You remember their face.
Their smile.
Their presence.
But one day the door opens.
They are standing in front of you.
Would you ignore the person because you were too busy holding the photograph?
Of course not.
The photograph mattered.
But the person was always greater.
That is the force of Paul's Christ-centered argument.
The shadow was not evil.
It served a purpose.
But the substance belongs to Christ.
And this is where some Christians become uncomfortable.
Because they fear that releasing a binding Sabbath requirement means abandoning God's holiness.
But what if the opposite danger also exists?
What if someone can become so consumed with defending a day that they lose sight of the Lord of that day?
That is not an accusation against sincere Sabbath observers.
Many seventh-day Sabbath-keeping Christians love Jesus deeply, affirm salvation by grace, and observe the day out of sincere conviction rather than an attempt to earn salvation.
We should honor that sincerity.
But no Christian, whatever their tradition, should allow a practice to become a substitute for the Savior.
Paul makes another striking statement in Romans 14:5–6.
"One man esteemeth one day above another: another esteemeth every day alike. Let every man be fully persuaded in his own mind."
He continues by saying that the person who regards the day does so to the Lord.
Some Christians understand this passage to address voluntary religious days or fasting practices rather than the weekly Sabbath.
Others understand its principle to include Sabbath observance.
Either way, Paul's concern is significant.
Believers must act with a conscience directed toward the Lord rather than treating disputable observances as grounds for contempt.
Romans 14 does not mean every biblical command becomes optional.
It does mean we should be extremely cautious about condemning fellow believers where the apostles did not authorize such condemnation.
And then Galatians 4:9–11 adds another warning.
Paul expresses concern over believers observing days, months, seasons, and years in a way connected to their return to spiritual bondage.
The problem was not that calendars are inherently sinful.
The problem was the religious significance these observances were acquiring within a distorted understanding of their relationship to God.
A person can rest on Saturday and glorify Christ.
A person can gather for worship on Sunday and glorify Christ.
A person can dedicate a particular day to prayer, service, and worship without believing that the day earns divine acceptance.
But when someone begins to say, Unless you observe my required day, you cannot be accepted by God, the Gospel itself is being placed in danger.
Because Scripture does not teach that sinners are justified by keeping the correct day of the week.
We are justified by God's grace through faith in Jesus Christ.
Ephesians 2:8–9 leaves no room for boasting.
Salvation is God's gift.
Not a religious achievement.
Not a reward for calendar accuracy.
Not a certificate issued to those who successfully performed enough sacred duties.
Our righteousness before God rests on Jesus Christ, not on the day we choose to rest.
But perhaps you are wondering about Sunday.
If the Sabbath was Saturday, who changed it to Sunday?
That question deserves a truthful answer.
The New Testament does not record a command from Jesus or the apostles explicitly transferring the seventh-day Sabbath obligation to the first day of the week.
We should not claim that it does.
The seventh day remains Saturday in the biblical weekly sequence.
Sunday is the first day of the week.
However, the New Testament records important first-day events.
Jesus rose from the dead on the first day of the week.
John 20:19 records the risen Jesus appearing to the gathered disciples that evening.
Acts 20:7 describes believers gathering to break bread on the first day of the week.
First Corinthians 16:2 instructs believers to set aside resources on the first day of every week, although the passage does not by itself establish a universal worship command.
Revelation 1:10 refers to the Lord's Day, which early Christian writers subsequently identify with Sunday, though the verse itself does not explicitly define the day.
These passages help explain the development of Sunday worship among Christians.
They do not establish that Sunday was simply renamed the seventh-day Sabbath.
This distinction matters.
A Christian who worships on Sunday should not pretend that Sunday is literally the seventh day.
And a Christian who worships on Saturday should not assume that every Sunday-worshiping believer is knowingly rebelling against God.
The earliest Christian communities developed their practices in a historical setting shaped by Jewish worship, the resurrection of Christ, and the growth of Gentile congregations.
Christians have since disagreed over the theological implications.
But no church has authority to rewrite Scripture.
Our convictions must be accountable to the Word of God.
Now consider the Jerusalem council in Acts 15.
Gentile believers were entering the church.
A major controversy erupted over whether they had to be circumcised and required to keep the law of Moses.
The apostles and elders gathered to address the matter.

The resulting letter instructed Gentile believers concerning particular practices necessary in that setting, but it did not impose weekly Sabbath observance as a condition of their inclusion among God's people.
This silence is not, by itself, conclusive proof that no Sabbath obligation could exist.
Arguments from silence must be handled carefully.
Yet it is significant when considered alongside Colossians 2, Romans 14, Galatians 4, and the New Testament's wider teaching about the new covenant.
The apostles were intensely concerned about holiness.
They condemned sexual immorality.
They commanded love.
They called believers to reject idolatry, dishonesty, greed, bitterness, and hatred.
They instructed churches to gather, encourage one another, pray, and persevere.
But they did not clearly establish seventh-day observance as a universal new-covenant condition of Christian faithfulness.
That should make us cautious about imposing such a condition ourselves.
And still, there is one more passage we must examine.
Perhaps the most beautiful of all.
Hebrews 4.
The writer speaks about God's rest, Israel's failure to enter it because of unbelief, and the promise that still remains for God's people.
Hebrews 4:9 says:
"There remaineth therefore a rest to the people of God."
The Greek word translated rest here is:
σαββατισμός
Sabbatismos.
It is a rare word associated with Sabbath rest or Sabbath celebration.
Some Christians argue that this wording supports continued weekly Sabbath observance.
Others understand it as describing the deeper Sabbath rest believers enter through faith in Christ, with its ultimate fulfillment still ahead.
The word itself does not settle the entire debate.
We must read the surrounding argument.
Hebrews 4:3 speaks of believers entering God's rest.
Hebrews 4:10 describes the one who has entered God's rest as resting from his works, just as God rested from His.
Hebrews 4:11 urges believers to be diligent to enter that rest.
The passage reaches beyond the question of a weekly calendar observance.
It concerns participation in God's promised rest through persevering faith.
And this brings us to the heart of the matter.
You can stop working for twenty-four hours and still have a soul that has never learned to rest in God.
You can close your business.
Turn off your phone.
Attend worship.
Refuse ordinary labor.
And still carry a crushing fear that you have not done enough to make God love you.
Perhaps that is the burden you have been carrying.
You pray, but wonder whether your prayers are sufficient.
You obey, but fear that one mistake has destroyed your standing before God.
You try to be holy, but your conscience never stops accusing you.
You keep looking for one more rule to satisfy.
One more religious achievement.
One more visible proof that you are acceptable.
And Jesus says in Matthew 11:28:
"Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest."
The Greek word for rest in this verse comes from ἀναπαύω (anapauō), meaning to give rest or refreshment.
Jesus was not merely offering exhausted people a better schedule.
He was inviting them to Himself.
To His gracious lordship.
To the One who carries the weary.
To the Savior whose yoke is easy and whose burden is light.
This does not mean following Jesus requires no sacrifice.
He calls us to deny ourselves, take up our cross, and follow Him.
But the cross we carry as disciples is not the same as trying to purchase our salvation through religious performance.
Jesus has already accomplished what no sinner could accomplish.
He lived in perfect obedience to the Father.
He bore our sins.
He died for the ungodly.
He rose again.
And He offers reconciliation with God to those who trust in Him.
At Calvary, the great issue was not whether a person had kept enough religious days.
The great issue was sin.
Our rebellion.
Our guilt.
Our alienation from a holy God.
And there, Jesus gave Himself for sinners.
The One who is Lord of the Sabbath entered death.
And on the first day of the week, the tomb was found empty.
Death had not conquered Him.
The resurrection announced that the crucified Messiah was alive.
And now the invitation goes out to every weary soul.
Come to Christ.
Not because obedience is worthless.
But because obedience cannot replace His saving work.
Not because God's holiness has diminished.
But because God's holiness and mercy meet in the crucified and risen Savior.
Not because repentance is unnecessary.
But because true repentance turns us away from sin and self-reliance toward the living Christ.
And that brings us to the answer many readers have been waiting for.
Must Christians observe a weekly seventh-day Sabbath as a binding command under the new covenant?

My conclusion, based on the New Testament evidence, is that Christians are not universally bound to observe the seventh-day Sabbath as a Mosaic covenant obligation, nor is Sabbath observance a condition of justification or salvation.

The clearest reasons are the Sabbath's covenantal role as a sign given to Israel, the fulfillment of the law's purposes in Christ, Paul's teaching concerning sacred days and Sabbaths, and the absence of an explicit apostolic command imposing seventh-day observance on all Gentile believers.
But this conclusion must be stated with humility.
Christians who understand the fourth commandment as continuing in a weekly Sabbath obligation have serious biblical arguments, especially from Genesis 2, Exodus 20, Matthew 5, and Hebrews 4.
Their interpretation should be engaged respectfully, not mocked or dismissed.
Nor does Christian freedom mean that rest, worship, and gathering with believers are unimportant.
Far from it.
God made us as creatures who need rest.
The church is called to gather and encourage one another.
Hebrews 10:24–25 warns believers against neglecting their assembling together.
Prayer matters.
Worship matters.
Time in Scripture matters.
Care for our families matters.
Mercy matters.

And a life consumed by endless labor, greed, entertainment, or distraction is not automatically a life of spiritual maturity simply because the believer claims freedom from the Mosaic Sabbath requirement.
Grace is not an excuse to neglect God.
Freedom from a covenantal obligation is not freedom from devotion to the Lord.
If you observe Saturday as a day of rest and worship out of sincere love for Christ, do so to the Lord.
If you gather on Sunday to celebrate the risen Savior, do so to the Lord.

If your circumstances require work on particular days, seek faithful rhythms of worship, rest, mercy, and Christian fellowship rather than surrendering to guilt over a requirement the New Testament does not clearly impose upon you.
And if you hold a strong Sabbath conviction, follow your conscience before God while continuing to examine Scripture carefully.
But please hear this.
Do not turn your calendar into a weapon against another believer.
Do not treat sincere obedience as something shameful.
Do not use grace as an excuse for indifference.
And do not allow a dispute over days to overshadow the One who died to reconcile us to God.
There are Christians who keep Saturday and love Jesus.
There are Christians who worship Sunday and love Jesus.
There are Christians who disagree about the fourth commandment yet stand together in confessing the same crucified and risen Lord.
The question that ultimately exposes the heart is not merely, Which day do you keep?
It is also:
Whom are you trusting to make you righteous before God?
Because if your answer is anything other than Jesus Christ, even the most disciplined religious life cannot save you.
Maybe you grew up terrified of breaking a rule.
Maybe you were taught that God was constantly waiting for you to fail.
Maybe you abandoned church because religious arguments made Christianity seem like an endless contest over who could prove everyone else wrong.
Or maybe you went to the opposite extreme.
You stopped taking obedience seriously.
You used grace to excuse habits that were slowly destroying your spiritual life.
And today, something in you knows that you need to return.
Not to religious fear.
Not to careless living.
But to Jesus.
The Jesus who forgives sinners.
The Jesus who calls His people to holiness.
The Jesus who restores the fallen.
The Jesus who confronts pride and welcomes the repentant.
The Jesus who does not need our self-righteousness to complete His sacrifice.
He calls us to believe, repent, and follow Him.
And perhaps the most important Sabbath question you will ever answer is this:
Have you entered the rest of trusting Christ, or are you still trying to save yourself?
If this article exposed a fear, challenged a conviction, or helped you understand God's Word more clearly, I would genuinely love to hear from you.

If you observe the seventh-day Sabbath, you are welcome here too. Tell us which passage most shapes your conviction. If you worship on Sunday, share how you understand the resurrection and the Lord's Day.
Let's have a conversation where Scripture is opened, questions are welcomed, and brothers and sisters are treated with dignity.
You do not have to pretend that every difficult biblical question has an easy answer.
But you can bring every question to the feet of Jesus.
And perhaps someone you know is quietly carrying the same confusion.
A parent who feels condemned.
A friend who has left church.
A believer who is exhausted by religious arguments.
A family member who sincerely wants to obey God but no longer knows whom to trust.
Because this ministry is not meant to build an audience around controversy.
It exists to point people toward Christ.
And that mission needs people who believe that sound biblical teaching, free resources, and Gospel-centered encouragement are worth sustaining.
These resources are offered to help people study Scripture, strengthen their faith, and grow in Christian maturity.
And if this ministry has helped you, I want to invite you into something deeper.
Second Corinthians 9:7 teaches that giving should be purposeful, willing, and cheerful, not reluctant or compelled.
You do not have to give money to earn His favor.
Christ has already accomplished our redemption.
But if you believe in this mission and have the means to help sustain it, your partnership can make a meaningful difference.
If this message has helped you see Jesus more clearly, consider becoming part of the community that helps keep this work moving forward.
Invite your family, your friends, the struggling believer, the person who has grown cold in faith, and even the seeker who has not yet come to know Christ.
Let them know that there is a place where they can encounter Scripture, wrestle with honest questions, and be continually pointed toward the Savior.
Because the world does not need another religious argument that leaves people more wounded than before.
It needs the truth of Jesus Christ proclaimed faithfully.
It needs repentance without self-righteousness.
Grace without compromise.
Conviction without cruelty.
Love without abandoning truth.
And Christians who understand that their greatest testimony is not how loudly they defend a particular day, but how faithfully they belong to the Lord of every day.
So whether you rest on Saturday, gather on Sunday, or are still studying what Scripture teaches, do not lose sight of the center.
Jesus Christ is Lord.
He is Lord of the Sabbath.
Lord of the church.
Lord of the living and the dead.
And He is the only Savior who can take a guilty sinner and make that person new.
One day, every argument will fall silent before Him.
Every proud religious achievement will lose its power to impress.
Every wounded conscience that has found refuge in His grace will discover the fullness of His promised rest.
And the question will no longer be whether we successfully defended our favorite position.
It will be whether we truly knew and trusted the One to whom the Scriptures testify.
The deepest rest your soul will ever know is not found in a day you managed to keep, but in the Savior who refused to let your sin have the final word.
